title: HTTPS and what encryption costs you
story:
Your bytes cross machines you do not control, and any of them can read what passes, alter it, or claim to be the other end. Three properties answer those three threats: confidentiality so the contents cannot be read, integrity so alteration is detected, and authentication so you know who you are talking to. The third is the one people forget, and it is the one that matters most — encryption to an attacker who has successfully impersonated your server is encryption working perfectly and protecting nobody.

What it costs is exchanges before any useful byte moves. The version specified in RFC 8446 in August 2018 reduced the full negotiation to a single round trip, by having the client speculatively send its key share in the first message so that encryption can begin after one exchange rather than two. It also mandates forward secrecy through ephemeral key exchange and removes the legacy cipher suites — forward secrecy meaning that recording today's traffic and stealing the long-term key later does not decrypt it, because the keys that actually protected the session no longer exist.

Then there is a mode that removes the last round trip, and it is worth understanding precisely because the trade is not obvious from the name. The specification is explicit about what is given up. That early data is not forward secret, since it is encrypted solely under keys derived from the offered pre-shared key. And there are no guarantees of non-replay between connections, because protection for ordinary data comes from the server's random value and this data does not depend on it.

Read the second one carefully, because it is a correctness problem rather than a cryptographic subtlety. An attacker who captures that early data can send it again, and the server has no way to know it is a repeat. The specification's requirement is a bound rather than a fix: any server instance — machine, thread or other entity in the serving infrastructure — must accept such early data for the same handshake at most once, which limits replays to the number of server instances in the deployment. So a fleet of two hundred servers means an attacker may be able to replay a captured request up to two hundred times.

Which produces a rule that is simple to state and frequently ignored. Only requests that are safe to execute repeatedly may travel in that mode. A read is fine. Anything that increments a counter, moves money or creates a record is not, and putting it there converts a performance optimisation into a duplicate-transaction bug that appears only under attack.

problem.name: Transport security
problem.shape: Bytes cross infrastructure you do not control, which can read them, alter them, or impersonate either end.
tell: a connection is being established to a new host on every request
latency is dominated by setup rather than by work
an early-data optimisation is being enabled globally
certificate verification is being disabled to make something work
problem.move: Reuse connections so the negotiation is amortised rather than repeated, and place services close to their callers because the cost is round trips and round trips are distance. If you enable the zero-round-trip mode, restrict it to requests that are safe to execute more than once, and never disable certificate verification to make a problem go away.
problem.invariant: The negotiation establishes confidentiality, integrity and authentication together. Encryption without authentication protects a conversation with whoever answered, which may be an attacker.
problem.breaks: The fastest mode is not simply faster. It gives up forward secrecy for the data it carries, and it carries no guarantee of non-replay between connections — the specification bounds replays to the number of server instances rather than preventing them, so a large fleet means a large replay budget.

cost.time: a round trip before useful data, amortised across a reused connection and paid again on every new one
cost.space: per-connection cryptographic state at both ends
cost.beats: an unencrypted connection, which is readable and modifiable by every intermediary, and application-level encryption, which usually authenticates nothing

worked.problem: What does the fastest mode of this protocol give up, and which requests may safely use it?
worked.reasoning:
Two properties, and only one of them is about cryptography — the other is a correctness problem that shows up as duplicated work.

The first is forward secrecy. Ordinary sessions use ephemeral key exchange, so recording traffic today and obtaining the long-term key later does not decrypt it, because the keys that protected the session no longer exist. Early data does not have this: the specification states it is not forward secret, since it is encrypted solely under keys derived from the offered pre-shared key. Anyone who captures that traffic and later compromises that key can read it.

The second is replay, and this is the one that changes what you may put there. The specification says plainly that there are no guarantees of non-replay between connections, because protection for ordinary data comes from the server's random value and early data does not depend on it. So an attacker who captures that data can send it again and the server cannot tell it is a repeat.

The mitigation in the specification is a bound rather than a prevention. Any server instance — machine, thread or other entity in the serving infrastructure — must accept such data for the same handshake at most once, which limits replays to the number of server instances in the deployment. That is a real constraint and it is not zero: a fleet of two hundred servers gives an attacker a budget of up to two hundred replays of a captured request.

So the rule is that only requests safe to execute repeatedly may travel that way. A read is fine — serving the same page a hundred times harms nothing. Anything that increments a counter, transfers money, sends a message or creates a record is not, because the duplicate is indistinguishable from a genuine second request and the failure appears only when somebody is attacking you, which is the worst time to discover it.

Two things I would add. The restriction has to be enforced by the server rather than assumed of the client, since an attacker chooses what to replay and will not respect your intentions about which requests belong in that mode. And the optimisation is worth less than it looks in most architectures, because reusing connections already amortises the handshake — the mode helps most for the first request to a host the client has spoken to before, which is a narrower case than the feature's framing suggests.

problem.practice: Check whether the zero-round-trip mode is enabled anywhere in your stack, and if it is, list which request paths can reach it. Then find one of those paths that changes state and work out what two executions of it would do.

beats.broke: The network carries your bytes past machines you do not control, any of which can read them, alter them, or pretend to be the other end.
beats.fix: Negotiate keys at the start of the connection and encrypt everything after, with certificates binding an identity to a key so the other end can be checked rather than assumed.
beats.cost: The negotiation is round trips before any useful byte moves, and the optimisation that removes the last round trip gives up forward secrecy and replay protection for the data it carries.

interview.q: What does the fastest mode of this protocol give up, and which requests may safely use it?
interview.trap: Treating it as a pure speed win with a cryptographic footnote. The replay property is a correctness problem — the specification bounds replays to the number of server instances rather than preventing them, so a state-changing request placed there is a duplicate-transaction bug that only appears under attack.
interview.answer:
Two properties, and only one is about cryptography — the other is a correctness problem that surfaces as duplicated work.

First, forward secrecy. Ordinary sessions use ephemeral key exchange, so capturing traffic today and obtaining the long-term key later does not decrypt it, because the protecting keys no longer exist. Early data lacks this: the specification says it is not forward secret, being encrypted solely under keys derived from the offered pre-shared key.

Second, replay, and this decides what may go there. The specification states there are no guarantees of non-replay between connections, because protection for ordinary data comes from the server's random value and early data does not depend on it. An attacker who captures it can send it again and the server cannot tell.

The mitigation is a bound rather than prevention: any server instance — machine, thread or other entity in the serving infrastructure — must accept it for the same handshake at most once, which limits replays to the number of server instances. That is real and it is not zero; a fleet of two hundred gives an attacker a budget of up to two hundred replays.

So only requests safe to execute repeatedly may use it. A read is fine. Anything incrementing a counter, moving money, sending a message or creating a record is not, because the duplicate is indistinguishable from a genuine second request and the failure appears only when someone is attacking you.

Two additions: the restriction must be enforced server-side, since an attacker chooses what to replay and will not respect your intentions about which requests belong there. And the optimisation is worth less than it appears, because reusing connections already amortises the handshake — it helps mainly on the first request to a previously contacted host.
